title: Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics
text:
Preface
These are the lecture notes for ASTRO 442, an introduction to the fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics of astrophysical systems. They are written to be self-contained: the textbook, Clarke and Carswell’s Principles of Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics (Clarke and Carswell 2007), is optional further reading. Each chapter ends with pointers to the relevant sections of the textbook.

How to use these notes

One chapter per lecture topic. The Schedule lists which chapter goes with each lecture.
Everything is numbered by chapter. Equation (9.14) is the fourteenth numbered equation of Chapter 9, and Exercise 8.4 is the fourth exercise of Chapter 8. When you ask a question about the notes, quote these numbers.
In-class worksheets appear near the end of each chapter, followed by the exercises. Homework assignments on Canvas list the exercises to solve, for example “Exercises 2.1, 7.3”.
Optional material is set apart in boxes titled “Going further”; you can skip it on a first reading.

title: 8  Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem
text:
8.1 The virial theorem
We consider a self-gravitating cloud of gas in equilibrium, described by the momentum equation \[
\frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho
\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] = - \rho \nabla \Psi,
\tag{8.1}\] where \(\Psi\) is the gravitational potential. We consider the scalar moment of inertia1 \[
I = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \rho (\mathbf{r}) r^2 \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{8.2}\] where \(V\) is a volume that encloses the whole gas cloud. The time derivative of \(I\) is (using the continuity equation) \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\frac{\mathrm{d} I}{\mathrm{d} t} &{}={} && \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \frac{\partial
\rho}{\partial t} r^2 \mathrm{d} V \\
&{}={} && - \frac{1}{2} \int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho
\mathbf{v}) r^2 \mathrm{d} V \\
&{}={} && - \frac{1}{2} \int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}r^2) \mathrm{d} V +
\frac{1}{2}  \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla r^2 \mathrm{d} V.
\end{alignedat}
\tag{8.3}\] The total divergence term is equal to a boundary integral \[
\int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}r^2) \mathrm{d} V = \int_S \rho
\mathbf{v}r^2 \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} S,
\tag{8.4}\] but the latter vanishes since, by assumption, \(\rho \rightarrow 0\) at the boundary of \(V\). So we find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} I}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla
r^2 \mathrm{d} V = \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{8.5}\] Here, we have used the fact that \(\nabla r =\mathbf{r}/ r\).
The second time derivative of \(I\) is \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 I}{\mathrm{d} t^2} &= \int_V \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V \\
&\qquad - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{r}) \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{r}] \mathrm{d} V \\
&\qquad + \int_V [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] : \nabla \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.6}\] Where the notation \(\mathbf{A}: \mathbf{B}\) denotes the inner product between two tensors: \[
\mathbf{A}: \mathbf{B}= \sum_{i = 1}^3 \sum_{k = 1}^3 A_{i k} B_{k i} =
\operatorname{Trace} \left[ \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
A_{x x} & A_{x y} & A_{x z}\\
A_{y x} & A_{y y} & A_{y z}\\
A_{z x} & A_{z y} & A_{z z}
\end{array}\right)  \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
B_{x x} & B_{x y} & B_{x z}\\
B_{y x} & B_{y y} & B_{y z}\\
B_{z x} & B_{z y} & B_{z z}
\end{array}\right) \right] .
\tag{8.7}\] Once again, we can drop the total divergence terms, since they vanish due to Gauss’ theorem, to find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 I}{\mathrm{d} t^2} = - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot
\mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V + \int_V [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+
p\mathbf{I}] : \nabla \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{8.8}\] The second term in the RHS is simpler than it looks, because \[
\nabla \mathbf{r}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\partial_x x & \partial_x y & \partial_x z\\
\partial_y x & \partial_y y & \partial_y z\\
\partial_z x & \partial_z y & \partial_z z
\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right) =\mathbf{I}.
\tag{8.9}\] So everything simplifies to \[
\int_V [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] : \nabla \mathbf{r}
\mathrm{d} V = \int_V \rho v^2 \mathrm{d} V + 3 \int_V p \mathrm{d} V =: 2 T +
3 \Pi,
\tag{8.10}\] where \(T\) is the kinetic energy of the gas and \(\Pi\) is the integrated pressure.
The first term in the RHS of Equation 8.8 requires a little more work. First, we need to compute an expression for the gravitational potential in terms of the mass density \(\rho\). To do this, we remember that the gravitational potential generated by a distribution of point masses with mass \(m_i\) at locations \(\mathbf{r}_i\) is given by \[
\Psi (\mathbf{r}) = - \sum_{i = 1}^N \frac{Gm_i}{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_i
|} .
\tag{8.11}\] This can be generalized to the case of a mass density distribution by converting the sum into an integral \[
\Psi (\mathbf{r}) = - \int_V \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}')}{ |
\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r}' .
\tag{8.12}\] Inserting this into the first term in the RHS of Equation 8.8 yields \[
\int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} = - \int_V
\mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \rho (\mathbf{r}) \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \int_V \mathrm{d}
\mathbf{r}'  \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}')}{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} \cdot
\mathbf{r},
\tag{8.13}\] where we have used the notation \(\nabla_{\mathbf{r}}\) to remind ourselves that the derivatives are computed with respect to the unprimed position \(\mathbf{r}\). In particular, note that \(\rho (\mathbf{r}')\) in the integral is not affected by the derivative, since it is a function of \(\mathbf{r}'\) and not of \(\mathbf{r}\). The only term that we need to differentiate is the denominator: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} \\
& \quad = \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + (z - z')^2}} \\
& \quad = \frac{- 1}{[(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + (z - z')^2]^{3 / 2}} \\
& \qquad\quad \times \left(\begin{array}{c}
x - x' \\
y - y' \\
z - z'
\end{array}\right) \\
& \quad = - \frac{\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'}{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.14}\] Inserting the last expression into Equation 8.13, we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
& \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \\
& \quad = \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r}' \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}') \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}') \cdot \mathbf{r} \\
& \quad = \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r}' \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}') \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}') \cdot (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}') \\
& \qquad\qquad + \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r}' \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}') \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}') \cdot \mathbf{r}' \\
& \quad = \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r}' \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}') \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} \\
& \qquad + \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r}' \rho (\mathbf{r}') \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}') \cdot \mathbf{r}' \\
& \quad = - \int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \Psi (\mathbf{r}) \rho (\mathbf{r}) - \int_V \rho (\mathbf{r}') \nabla_{\mathbf{r}'} \Psi (\mathbf{r}') \cdot \mathbf{r}' \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r}' .
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.15}\] We have used the fact that (note the difference in sign compared to Equation 8.14) \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{r}'}  \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} =
\frac{\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'}{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} .
\tag{8.16}\] The last term on the RHS of Equation 8.15 is identical to the LHS, so we find \[
- \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r}= \frac{1}{2}
\int_V \mathrm{d} \mathbf{r} \Psi (\mathbf{r}) \rho (\mathbf{r}) = \Omega,
\tag{8.17}\] \(\Omega\) being the gravitational potential energy.
For a stationary configuration \(\mathrm{d}^2 I / \mathrm{d} t^2 = 0\), so Equation 8.8 yields the virial theorem: \[
\boxed{\Omega + 2 T + 3 \Pi = 0.}
\tag{8.18}\] For an ideal gas \(p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon\), so \[
\Pi = \int_V p \mathrm{d} V = (\Gamma - 1) \int_V \rho \varepsilon \mathrm{d} V =
(\Gamma - 1) U,
\tag{8.19}\] where \(U\) is the total internal energy. In this case, the virial theorem reads \[
\boxed{\Omega + 2 T + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.}
\tag{8.20}\]

title: 8  Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem
text:
8.2 Hydrostatic equilibria
The virial theorem has an important consequence for the stability of hydrostatic equilibria. Consider a cloud of gas or star in hydrostatic equilibrium, that is with no large scale motion (no rotation). Then the virial theorem states that \[
\Omega + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.
\tag{8.21}\] On the other hand, the energy of the cloud is \[
E = \Omega + U.
\tag{8.22}\] The energy must be negative for the system to be stable \(E \leq 0\). This implies \[
U \leq - \Omega = 3 (\Gamma - 1) U \Longrightarrow [- 1 + 3 (\Gamma -
1)] U \geq 0,
\tag{8.23}\] since \(U \geq 0\), this requires \[
\Gamma \geq 4 / 3.
\tag{8.24}\] Monoatomic gas has \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\), so regular stars are stable. White dwarfs close to their maximum mass and very hot stars that are radiation pressure dominated have \(\Gamma \approx 4 / 3\), so they are unstable. They explode as Type Ia supernovae and pair-instability supernova, respectively.
A surprising consequence of the virial theorem is that self-gravitating systems have negative specific heat. Consider a self-gravitating cloud (a protostar) emitting infrared radiation. As its energy \(E\) becomes more negative its gravitational binding energy \(- \Omega\) must increase, because \(U \geq 0\). We can use Equation 8.21 and Equation 8.22 to solve for \(U\) in terms of \(E\): \[
U = - \frac{E}{3 \Gamma - 4} .
\tag{8.25}\] If \(\Gamma > 4 / 3\), Equation 8.25 predicts that \(U\) will increase as \(E\) becomes more negative. Meaning that the system heats up as it loses energy! Eventually the cloud contracts to the point that nuclear fusion starts occurring and a star is born. Nuclear burning prevents the star from heating up further.

title: 8  Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem
text:
8.3 Application to star formation
Consider a spherical cloud of radius \(R\). Let the typical density be \(\bar{\rho}\). Then the gravitational potential energy is (neglecting factors of order unity) \[
- \Omega = G \int_0^R 4 \pi r \rho (r) \mathcal{M} (r) \mathrm{d} r \approx (4
\pi)^2 G \bar{\rho}^2 R^5,
\tag{8.26}\] where \[
\mathcal{M} (r) = \int_0^r 4 \pi r^2 \rho (r) \mathrm{d} r.
\tag{8.27}\] For an ideal gas, the pressure is given by \[
p = \frac{k_B T}{Am_p} \rho,
\tag{8.28}\] where \(A\) is the atomic mass unit of the gas in units of the proton mass \(m_p\), \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant and \(T\) is the temperature. We can assume \(T\) to be constant. This is a good approximation for optically thin clouds which can efficiently cool by emitting radiation. With this approximation \[
\Pi = \int_0^R 4 \pi r^2 p (r) \mathrm{d} r \approx \frac{4}{3} \pi c_s^2
\bar{\rho} R^3,
\tag{8.29}\] where \[
c_s^2 = \frac{k_B T}{Am_p}
\tag{8.30}\] is a constant. As we will see later, \(c_s\) turns out to be the sound speed of the gas. The condition for collapse of the cloud is that \(3 \Pi < | \Omega |\), which implies that collapse will occur for a cloud with \[
R > R_J, \qquad R_J^2 = \frac{c_s^2}{4 \pi \bar{\rho} G} .
\tag{8.31}\] This is called the Jeans length. Typical molecular clouds have \(R \gg R_J\). So instead of collapsing to an object with mass equal to the mass of the cloud, they fragment into smaller stars. The mass of these protostars can be estimated as the mass contained within one Jeans radius, the so-called Jeans mass2: \[
M_J = \frac{4 \pi}{3}  \bar{\rho} R_J^3 = \frac{c_s^3}{3 (4 \pi
\bar{\rho})^{1 / 2} G^{3 / 2}} = \frac{k_B^{3 / 2}}{3 (4 \pi)^{1 / 2} m_p^2
G^{3 / 2}}  \frac{T^{3 / 2}}{A^2 n^{1 / 2}} .
\tag{8.32}\] In CGS units the Jeans mass is \[
M_J \approx 1.59 M_{\odot}  \left( \frac{T}{\mathrm{K}} \right)^{3 / 2}
\left( \frac{\operatorname{cm}^{- 3}}{n} \right)^{1 / 2}  \frac{1}{A^2} .
\tag{8.33}\] For a typical molecular cloud with \(T = 10\,\mathrm{K}\), \(n = 100 \operatorname{cm}^{- 3}\), and \(A = 2\) (for molecular hydrogen) the Jeans mass is \(M_J \approx 1.25 M_{\odot}\), giving a reasonable estimate for the typical mass of a fragment of the cloud. Note however that the Jeans mass decreases with increasing \(n\), so, if the gas can efficiently cool, the cloud might undergo further fragmentation forming clusters of small stars.
While the arguments we have given here give an order of magnitude estimate for the mass of protostars, star formation is strongly influenced by a number of factors that we have neglected. These include turbulence and magnetic fields. Moreover, star formation strongly depends on the ability of the gas to cool to low temperature, as shown by Equation 8.33.

8.5 Exercises

Exercise 8.1 (Self-gravitating slab) An infinite, static slab of incompressible fluid with uniform density \(\rho_0\) fills the region \(| z | < a\) and is held together by its own gravity.

Compute the gravitational acceleration inside and outside the slab, and the pressure profile inside it.
Model the disk of a galaxy as such a slab, with \(\rho_0 = 10^{-21}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\) and \(a = 10^{20}\,\mathrm{cm}\). A star starts at rest at \(z = a\). How fast does it cross the mid-plane, and what is the period of its vertical oscillation?

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 8.


Exercise 8.2 (Mass of a molecular cloud) A self-gravitating cloud of molecular hydrogen \(\left( p = nk_B T = \frac{2}{5} \rho \varepsilon \right)\) is measured to have radius \(R = 0.1 \operatorname{pc}\) and temperature \(T = 10\mathrm{K}\). Estimate the mass of the cloud.


Exercise 8.3 (Temperature of the solar core) Estimate the temperature at the centre of the Sun, assuming that density and pressure change over a length scale comparable to the solar radius. Make the estimate twice: first assuming that the Sun is supported by gas pressure, then assuming that it is supported by radiation pressure. Which assumption is more plausible, and why?
Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 11.

Plot the solution for \(n = 1.5\) and find the radius of the polytrope, i.e., the value \(\xi_r\) at which \(\theta (\xi_r) = 0\).

title: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect
text:
9.1 Oscillation Equation
The equations of fluid mechanics are nonlinear and only few analytic solutions are known. However, significant insight into astrophysical systems can be obtained by considering small perturbations around a background flow. Typically the background is chosen to be a hydrostatic solution, e.g., the density profile of an atmosphere. However, this method can be applied to more general situations. This is the key working principle of astroseismology. Sound waves are also one of the key tools to learn about the early Universe, as they generate the baryonic-acoustics oscillations seen in the CMB.
To set the stage, consider a gas flow with density, pressure, and velocity \[
\rho_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad p_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad \mathbf{v}_0 (t
; \mathcal{V}) .
\tag{9.1}\] We describe its perturbation in terms of a small displacement vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t ; \mathcal{V})\) describing the offset of each fluid element from its background state.
The density, pressure, and velocity of each fluid element change according to \[
\rho (t ; \mathcal{V}) = \rho_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}) + \delta \rho (t ;
\mathcal{V}), \quad p (t ; \mathcal{V}) = p_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}) + \delta p
(t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad \mathbf{v} (t ; \mathcal{V}) =\mathbf{v}_0 (t ;
\mathcal{V}) + \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi} (t ; \mathcal{V})}{\mathrm{d} t} .
\tag{9.2}\] The quantities with the \(\delta\) in front are the Lagrangian perturbations1. The Eulerian perturbation of a quantity is given by \[
q' (t, \mathbf{x}) = q_0 (t, \mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\xi}) + \delta q (t,
\mathbf{x}) - q_0 (t, \mathbf{x}) = \delta q (t, \mathbf{x}) -\boldsymbol{\xi}
\cdot \nabla q_0 .
\tag{9.3}\] The difference between Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations, is that the Lagrangian perturbations are specific to individual fluid elements, while the Eulerian perturbations record the difference in the flow at a fixed position. This distinction turns out to be crucial when perturbing non-homogeneous backgrounds, for which \(\nabla q_0 \neq 0\), as we will see later.
For the moment, we consider an homogeneous medium in which \(\rho_0\), \(p_0\), and \(\mathbf{v}_0 = 0\) are constant. We perturb it by displacing the fluid elements by a small amount \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) and let it evolve freely. How do the perturbations evolve? To find out, we need to insert the Lagrangian perturbations into the Lagrangian equations.
The continuity equation reads \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}
\longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} (\rho_0 + \delta \rho )}{\mathrm{d} t} = - (\rho_0
+ \delta \rho) \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t}
\right) .
\tag{9.4}\] Dropping quantities that are quadratic or higher order in the perturbation, we obtain \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \delta \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \longrightarrow \boxed{\delta \rho = - \rho_0
\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}} .
\tag{9.5}\] To find the perturbed momentum equation, first note that \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial
t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}= \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}+ \left(
\frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot \nabla \right) \boldsymbol{\xi}=
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + o (| \boldsymbol{\xi} |),
\tag{9.6}\] so \[
\mathbf{v}= \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}
\mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}+ \left( \frac{\mathrm{d}
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot \nabla \right) \mathbf{v}= \frac{\partial^2
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} + o (| \boldsymbol{\xi} |) .
\tag{9.7}\] The momentum equation becomes \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p \rightarrow
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \frac{1}{\rho_0} \nabla p =
- \frac{1}{\rho_0} \nabla \delta p.
\tag{9.8}\] We will consider only the case of adiabatic perturbations, for which \[
p = p (\rho) .
\tag{9.9}\] In other words, we are taking the pressure at constant entropy. For example, for an ideal-gas, we have already seen that for adiabatic processes \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon \longrightarrow p = K \rho^{\Gamma} .
\tag{9.10}\] with \(K = (\Gamma - 1) \rho^{1 - \Gamma} \varepsilon\).
In this case, we can use the chain rule to rewrite \(\nabla \delta p\) in terms of \(\nabla \delta \rho\): \[
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \frac{1}{\rho_0}
\frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} \rho} \nabla \delta \rho = \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d}
\rho} \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{9.11}\] Defining the sound speed \(c_s = \sqrt{\mathrm{d} p / \mathrm{d} \rho}\), we obtain the oscillation equation: \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2 \nabla
\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}= 0.}
\tag{9.12}\] In general, the sound speed needs to be evaluated at constant entropy, that is \[
\boxed{c_s = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s} .}
\tag{9.13}\]
The oscillation Equation 9.12 is the fundamental equation to describe sound waves. Taking the divergence on both sides and using Equation 9.5, we find that the density perturbation \(\delta \rho\) satisfies the wave equation: \[
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2 \nabla^2 \delta \rho =
0.
\tag{9.15}\] To solve the oscillation equation, we consider the ansatz \[
\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \exp [\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}-
\omega t)],
\tag{9.16}\] which describes a plane sound wave propagating in the direction \(\mathbf{k}\) and having frequency \(\omega\). \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1\) is the polarization vector, describing the way in which fluid elements oscillates as the wave propagates. Inserting this ansatz into Equation 9.12, we find \[
\omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = c_s^2 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1)
.
\tag{9.17}\] This means that plane wave solutions to Equation 9.12 exist only for specific choices of \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1, \omega\) and \(\mathbf{k}\). This is an example of dispersion relation. We see that the RHS is parallel to \(\mathbf{k}\), so solutions can exist only if \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \parallel \mathbf{k}\). This means that sound waves are longitudinal. This is opposite from electromagnetic waves in vacuum, in which the electric and magnetic fields oscillate in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Setting \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = \xi_1 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\), we find \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2 k^2 .
\tag{9.18}\] This means that both phase and group velocity for sound waves is given by \(c_s\) \[
v_{\operatorname{phase}} = \frac{\omega}{k} = c_s, \qquad v_{\operatorname{group}} =
\frac{\mathrm{d} \omega}{\mathrm{d} k} = c_s .
\tag{9.19}\] This justifies the name sound speed for \(c_s\).
What happens to fluid elements when a sound wave passes through them? They are displaced along the direction of the wave. This causes a compression of the fluid. From Equation 9.5, we find: \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0  (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1) e^{\mathrm{i}
(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} .
\tag{9.20}\]

For an ideal-gas, with \(p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon = \frac{\rho}{\mu} k_B T\), the pressure at constant entropy is \[
c_s^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \Gamma K
\rho^{\Gamma - 1} = (\Gamma - 1) \Gamma \varepsilon = \frac{\Gamma k_B
T}{\mu} .
\tag{9.14}\]

Consider a sound wave propagating along \(z\) with wavelength \(\lambda = 1\). Then \(\mathbf{k}= k \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right)^T\) and \(\omega = c_s\). The only non-zero component of \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is the \(z\)-component \[
\xi_z = \xi_1 e^{\mathrm{i} (z - c_s t)} = A \cos [k (z - c_s t)] + B \sin [k
(z - c_s t)] \Longleftrightarrow \xi_1 = A - \mathrm{i} B
\tag{9.21}\] The density perturbation is given by \[
\frac{\delta \rho}{\rho_0} = - \frac{\partial \xi_z}{\partial z} = k \{ A
\sin [k (z - c_s t)] - B \cos [k (z - c_s t)] \} .
\tag{9.22}\]

9.2 Wave Energy and Momentum
Sound waves also transport energy and momentum. The deposition of energy by breaking waves is thought to play an important role in phenomena such as core-collapse supernovae, stellar eruptions, and the evolution of giant molecular clouds.






NoteGoing further: Normal Modes



Before we can compute the energy carried by waves, we need to develop some general perturbation theory. In general, the oscillation equation takes the form \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\xi},
\tag{9.23}\] where \(\hat{\mathbf{F}}\) is a differential operator. For example, for sound waves in a homogeneous medium \(\hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\xi}= \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}\). We can find a dispersion relation by looking for solutions such that \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) e^{- \mathrm{i}
\omega t} .
\tag{9.24}\] Inserting this ansatz in Equation 9.23, we find an eigenvalue problem \[
- \omega^2 \rho_0 \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) .
\tag{9.25}\] In most applications, \(\hat{\mathbf{F}}\) is self-adjoint: \[
\int \boldsymbol{\zeta} (\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\xi}
(\mathbf{x}) \rho_0 (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{x}= \int \boldsymbol{\xi}
(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\zeta} (\mathbf{x}) \rho_0
(\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{x}.
\tag{9.26}\] The general theory of linear operators then implies that Equation 9.25 has an infinite set of eigenvalues \(\{ \omega_n \}\) and eigenfunctions \(\{ \boldsymbol{\eta}_n \}\) and that any perturbation (not just plane waves) can be written as an infinite superposition of elementary solutions: \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \sum_n \boldsymbol{\eta}_n (\mathbf{x}) e^{-
i \omega_n t} .
\tag{9.27}\] The quantities \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_n (\mathbf{x})\) are also called the normal modes of oscillations. Note that the normal modes need not be countable. For example, for sound waves in a homogeneous infinite medium all positive sound frequencies \(\omega\) are allowed. In this case, Equation 9.27 takes the form of an integral. For plane waves in a homogeneous medium, Equation 9.27 is just the Fourier transform: \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}\boldsymbol{\eta}
(\mathbf{k}) e^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}} e^{- \mathrm{i} c_s kt} .
\tag{9.28}\] However, when we consider sound waves in a finite medium, for example a star of a given radius, the requirement that standing wave solutions have a wavelength that is an integer fraction of the dimension of the star, makes the frequencies \(\{ \omega_n \}\) quantized.






TipExample



Consider a rigid, cylindrical pipe of length \(L\) filled with gas at constant density and temperature. The ends of the pipe are sealed. The displacement equation for sound waves propagating in the pipe is \[
\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\partial_t^2 \xi (t, z) = c_s^2 \partial_z^2 \xi (t, z), & 0 < z < L,\\
\xi (t, 0) = \xi (t, L) = 0. &
\end{array}\right.
\tag{9.29}\] If we look for solutions in the form \(\xi (t, z) = \eta (z) e^{\mathrm{i} \omega t}\), we find the eigenvalue problem \[
\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\partial_z^2 \eta (z) + \left( \frac{\omega}{c_s} \right)^2 \eta (z) =
0, & 0 < z < L\\
\eta (0) = \eta (L) = 0. &
\end{array}\right.
\tag{9.30}\] This equation is just the equation for a harmonic oscillator. The general solution is \[
\eta (z) = A \cos (\kappa z) + B \sin (\kappa z), \qquad \kappa =
\frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{9.31}\] However, not all solutions satisfy the boundary conditions. To satisfy the boundary conditions, we require \[
A = 0, \qquad \kappa = \frac{n \pi}{L} \Longrightarrow \omega = c_s
\left( \frac{n \pi}{L} \right), \quad n = 1, 2, \ldots
\tag{9.32}\] The first few normal modes are plotted in Figure 9.2.






Figure 9.2: Normal modes for gas in a cylindrical pipe.



This means that all sound waves propagating along the pipe are in the form \[
\xi (t, z) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \left[ A_n \sin \left( \frac{n \pi c_s
t}{L} \right) + B_n \cos \left( \frac{n \pi c_s t}{L} \right) \right] \sin
\left( \frac{n \pi z}{L} \right),
\tag{9.33}\] where \(A_n, B_n\) are determined by the initial conditions \(\xi (t = 0, z)\).










NoteGoing further: Work Integral



We might be tempted to define the energy density of a wave in the general form \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) e^{\mathrm{i} \omega t}\) as \[
K_{\operatorname{wave}} = \frac{1}{2} \rho_0  \left\langle \left| \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t } \right|^2 \right\rangle = \frac{1}{2} \rho_0  |
\boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \langle | \omega \sin (\omega t) |^2 \rangle =
\frac{\omega}{4} \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2,
\tag{9.34}\] where \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) denotes averaging over a period \(T = 2 \pi / \omega\) of the wave. Equation 9.34 is the kinetic energy associated with the wave. However, it turns out that the kinetic energy is just one portion of the wave energy.
The energy of the wave is related to \(\xi^2\), so it cannot be computed directly from linear theory. However, we can use a trick:

adiabatically perturb the system to create a wave with an external force;
compute the work done by the external force on the system.

To achieve this we add a source term to the oscillation equation: \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\xi}+\mathbf{F}_{\operatorname{ext}} (t) .
\tag{9.35}\] Suppose we want to excite the mode \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) e^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) is such that \(\hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\eta}= - \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\eta}\). Then we can take \(\mathbf{F}_{\operatorname{ext}} (t) = F_0 e^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x})\), where \(F_0\) is chosen so that for \(t \lesssim 0\), \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = e^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x})\). Inserting this into the oscillation equation yields \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \rho_0 \gamma^2
e^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}= e^{\gamma t}  \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\eta}+ F_0 e^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}= (- \rho_0 \omega^2 + F_0)
e^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}.
\tag{9.36}\] We can solve for \(F_0\) to find that \[
F_0 = \rho_0  (\omega^2 + \gamma^2) .
\tag{9.37}\] The work done by the external force per unit volume is given by the work integral \[
W = \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t}
\cdot \mathbf{F}_{\operatorname{ext}} = \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \rho_0 \gamma
(\gamma^2 + \omega^2) e^{2 \gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta}=
\rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \gamma (\gamma^2 +
\omega^2) e^{2 \gamma t},
\tag{9.38}\] where we have used the fact that \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) is time independent. The last integral can be computed analytically, so the previous expression yields \[
W = \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \left( \frac{\gamma^2}{2} +
\frac{\omega^2}{2} \right) .
\tag{9.39}\] The energy of the wave is obtained in the limit in which \(\gamma \downarrow 0\): \[
\boxed{E_{\operatorname{wave}} = \frac{\omega}{2} \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2
.}
\tag{9.40}\] Note that \(E_{\operatorname{wave}} = 2 K_{\operatorname{wave}}\), meaning that half of the wave energy is potential energy. For example, for a sound wave with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}=\mathbf{A} \cos (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x})\), the mean energy density (averaging over one wave-length) is \[
E_{\operatorname{wave}} = \frac{\omega}{4} \rho_0 A^2 .
\tag{9.41}\] It is possible to compute the linear momentum \(\mathbf{P}_{\operatorname{wave}}\) carried by waves in a similar way. One finds \[
\boxed{\mathbf{P}_{\operatorname{wave}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{\omega}
E_{\operatorname{wave}} .}
\tag{9.42}\]

10.1 Waves in Isothermal Atmospheres
Consider a stratified, static, isothermal atmosphere. We assume constant acceleration \(g\) in the negative \(z\) direction. The hydrostatic equilibrium equations are \[
\partial_z p_0 = - \rho_0 g, \qquad p = a^2 \rho,
\tag{10.1}\] where \(a = \sqrt{\frac{kT}{\mu}}\) is the isothermal sound speed.
Combining these two we find \[
\partial_z \rho_0 = - \frac{g}{a ^2} \rho_0 \Longrightarrow \rho_0 =
\tilde{\rho} e^{- z / H} .
\tag{10.2}\] \(H = a^2 / g\) is called the scale-high of the atmosphere and has units of a length.
We want to study the propagation of waves in this atmosphere. The continuity equation still gives \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{10.3}\] and the velocity perturbation is \[
\mathbf{v}' = \delta \mathbf{v}- (\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}_0 =
\delta \mathbf{v}= \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}=
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} .
\tag{10.4}\] The sound speed is given by \[
c_s^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \Gamma a^2 .
\tag{10.5}\] Which implies that \(\delta p = \Gamma a^2 \delta \rho\) for adiabatic perturbations. However, \[
p' \overset{!}{=} \Gamma a^2 \rho',
\tag{10.6}\] instead we have \[
\delta p = \Gamma a^2 \delta \rho \Longrightarrow (p' +\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot
\nabla p_0) = \Gamma a^2 \delta \rho \Longrightarrow p' = \Gamma a^2 \delta
\rho + g \rho_0 \xi_z .
\tag{10.7}\] The momentum equation reads \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p - g \rho
\hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.8}\] Setting \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}'\), \(p = p_0 + p'\), and \(\rho = \rho_0 + \rho'\) yields \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \nabla p_0 - g
\rho_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \nabla p' - g \rho'  \hat{\mathbf{z}} +
\operatorname{HOT} .
\tag{10.9}\] The first two terms on the RHS cancel out. Dropping the higher order terms we find \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \Gamma a^2 \nabla
\delta \rho + g \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - g \rho_0 \nabla
\xi_z - g \left( \delta \rho + \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z  \right)
\hat{\mathbf{z}},
\tag{10.10}\] where we have used Equation 10.7 and \[
\rho' = \delta \rho - (\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \nabla) \rho_0 = \delta r +
\frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z .
\tag{10.11}\] The second and last term on the RHS of Equation 10.10 cancel out leaving \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \Gamma a^2 \nabla
\delta \rho - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z - g \delta \rho \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.12}\] Using the fact that \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \delta \rho &= \nabla (- \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
&= - \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \nabla \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \\
&= - \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}+ \frac{\rho_0}{H} \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.13}\] We obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_0 \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {}& \Gamma a^2 \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \rho_0 \Gamma g \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\
& - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z + g \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.14}\] This can be simplified to \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {}& c_s^2 \left( \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \frac{a^2}{c_s^2} \frac{1}{H} \nabla \xi_z \right) \\
& - \frac{(c_s^2 - a^2)}{H} \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{10.15}\] We are going to analyze the consequences of this equation shortly. Before we do that, we show that this equation reduces to Eq. (6.31) of Clarke and Carswell (2007) in the limit of vertical oscillations in the \(z\) direction. To do that, we take the divergence of Equation 10.15 to obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} &= c_s^2 \left( \nabla^2 \delta \rho + \frac{\delta \rho}{H^2} \right) + g \rho_0 \nabla^2 \xi_z \\
&\qquad - \frac{(c_s^2 - a^2)}{H} \left( \partial_z \delta \rho + \frac{\delta \rho}{H} \right) \\
&= c_s^2 \nabla^2 \delta \rho - \frac{c_s^2}{H} \partial_z \delta \rho + \frac{a^2}{H} \rho_0 \nabla^2 \xi_z \\
&\qquad + \frac{a^2}{H} \partial_z \delta \rho + a^2 \frac{\delta \rho}{H^2} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.16}\] Assuming that \(\delta \rho = \delta \rho (t, z)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}= \xi_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), we obtain, \[
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2  \frac{\partial^2 \delta
\rho}{\partial z^2} - \frac{c_s^2}{H}  \frac{\partial \delta \rho}{\partial
z} = 0,
\tag{10.17}\] where we have used the fact that \[
\nabla^2 \xi_z = \partial_z^2 \xi_z = \partial_z  \left( - \frac{\delta
\rho}{\rho_0} \right) = - \frac{\partial_z \delta \rho}{\rho_0} -
\frac{\delta \rho}{\rho_0 H} .
\tag{10.18}\] Equation 10.17 is identical to Eq. (6.31) of Clarke and Carswell (2007). It describes the propagation of density modes in a stratified atmosphere, but neglects an entirely different class of modes that have \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) in the z-direction, but propagate in the xy-plane.
As before, we look for traveling wave solutions \[
\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\eta}e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}
.
\tag{10.19}\] Inserting this into Equation 10.15 we obtain \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\omega^2 \boldsymbol{\eta} = {}& c_s^2 \left( \mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta}+ \mathrm{i} \frac{a^2}{c_s^2} \frac{1}{H} \eta_z \right) \mathbf{k} \\
& + \mathrm{i} \frac{(c_s^2 - a^2)}{H} \mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{10.20}\]

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
In the limit of \(H \gg a^2 k / \omega^2\), that is, in the limit in which the wavelength of perturbations is much smaller than the scale height of the atmosphere, we recover the dispersion relation for waves in a homogeneous medium, namely \(\omega^2 = c_s k^2\), as expected.
Purely horizontal waves, with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}, \mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{z}}\) cannot satisfy the dispersion relation, unless \(c_s = a\), that is for isothermal as opposed to adiabatic perturbations. Physically this means that density fluctuations become buoyant, so they acquire a \(k_z \neq 0\) component in their wave vector.
Waves with \(\boldsymbol{\eta} \parallel \mathbf{k} \parallel \hat{\mathbf{z}}\) satisfy the dispersion relation simplifies to \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2  \left( k^2 + \mathrm{i} \frac{1}{H} k \right)
\Longrightarrow k_{1, 2} = - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2 H} \pm \sqrt{\left(
\frac{\omega}{c_s} \right)^2 - \left( \frac{1}{2 H} \right)^2} .
\tag{10.21}\] These are the so called pressure or p-modes of the atmosphere. They are the generalization of sound waves.

If \(H \gg \frac{c_s}{\omega}\), then the dispersion relation for p-modes can be approximated as: \[
k_{1, 2} \approx - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2 H} \pm \frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{10.22}\] In this case the displacement grows exponentially with height: \[
\xi_z = \eta_z e^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} =
\eta_z \exp \left[ \mathrm{i} \omega \left( \pm \frac{z}{c_s} - t \right)
\right] \exp \left( \frac{z}{2 H} \right) .
\tag{10.23}\] This means that waves propagating vertically along an isothermal atmosphere eventually become nonlinear and will experience wave-breaking. Note that the density fluctuation remains finite: \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}= - \tilde{\rho} \eta_z
\left( \frac{\mathrm{i} \omega}{c_s} + \frac{1}{2 H} \right) \exp \left[
\mathrm{i} \omega \left( \frac{z}{c_s} - t \right) \right] \exp \left( -
\frac{z}{2 H} \right) .
\tag{10.24}\]
If \(H \ll \frac{c_s}{\omega}\), then the solution describes one of two global oscillation modes of the atmosphere: \[
k_{1, 2} \approx - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{H}, 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
[\xi_z]_{1, 2} = \eta  e^{\mathrm{i} \omega t}, \eta_z e^{z / H} e^{\mathrm{i}
\omega t} .
\tag{10.25}\]

Let us now consider the case of perturbations with horizontal displacement. We can align the \(x\)-axis with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\), meaning that \(\boldsymbol{\eta}= \eta \hat{\mathbf{x}}\). In this case, the dispersion relation becomes \[
\omega^2 \eta \hat{\mathbf{x}} = c_s^2  (k_x \eta) \mathbf{k}+ \mathrm{i}
\frac{(c_s^2 - a^2)}{H} k_x \eta \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.26}\] This means that there are two components of \(\mathbf{k}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc} k_x & 0 & k_z \end{array}\right)\). The x-component of Equation 10.26 is \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2 k_x^2 \Longrightarrow k_x = \pm \frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{10.27}\] The \(z\)-component of Equation 10.26 is \[
k_z = - \mathrm{i} \left( 1 - \frac{a^2}{c_s^2} \right)  \frac{1}{H} .
\tag{10.28}\] The corresponding displacement is \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \eta \exp \left[ \mathrm{i} \omega \left( \pm
\frac{x}{c_s} - t \right) \right] \exp \left[ \left( 1 - \frac{a^2}{c_s^2}
\right)  \frac{z}{H} \right]  \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{10.29}\] Note that, as in the previous case, the density fluctuations \(\delta \rho\) remain finite. These are the so called (internal) gravity-modes or g-modes of the atmosphere. In the limit in which \(c_s \rightarrow a\), that is \(\Gamma \rightarrow 1\) (isothermal perturbations), these type of waves reduce to horizontal sound waves.

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.2 In-class worksheet
We consider small disturbances in a plane parallel, isothermal atmosphere. We will assume \(z\) to be the vertical direction and \(g\) to be the gravitational acceleration, assumed to be constant and towards the negative \(z\) direction. Let \(a = \sqrt{k_B T / \mu}\) be the isothermal sound speed.

Show that the static background density \(\rho_0\) satisfies \[
\rho_0 (z) = \tilde{\rho} e^{- z / H},
\tag{10.30}\] where \(H = a^2 / g\) is the scale height of the atmosphere.
Let \(\delta \rho\) and \(\rho'\) be the Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations of the density. Show that \[
\rho' = \delta \rho + \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z .
\tag{10.31}\]
Let \(p'\) be the Eulerian pressure perturbation. Show that \[
p' = c_s^2 \delta \rho + g \rho_0 \xi_z,
\tag{10.32}\] where \(c_s^2 = \Gamma a^2\) is the square of the sound speed and \(\xi_z\) is the \(z\)-component of the displacement.
Use the results from the previous two points to show that \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - c_s^2 \nabla
\delta \rho - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z - g \delta \rho \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.33}\]

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.3 Exercises

Exercise 10.1 (Waves in a polytropic atmosphere) An isentropic atmosphere sits in a uniform gravitational field \(g\), with pressure \(p_0 = A \rho_0^{1 + 1/n}\) and \(A\) constant. Let \(x\) be the depth below the top of the atmosphere, and suppose that the unperturbed density is \(\rho_0 = (kx)^n\) with \(k\) constant.

Show that hydrostatic equilibrium requires \(g = Ak (1 + n)\).
Perturb the atmosphere with a small vertical velocity \(u\), taken positive upward, together with adiabatic perturbations \(p' \ll p_0\) of the pressure and \(\rho' \ll \rho_0\) of the density. Show that \(p' = (gx / n) \rho'\).
Show that the linearized continuity and momentum equations are \[
\frac{\partial \rho'}{\partial t} - u \frac{\partial \rho_0}{\partial x} - \rho_0 \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0
\tag{10.34}\] and \[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \left( \frac{\rho'}{\rho_0} \right) g - \frac{g}{n \rho_0} \frac{\partial (x \rho')}{\partial x} = 0.
\tag{10.35}\]
For \(n = 1/2\), combine these equations to show that \[
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = 2 gx \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + 3 g \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} .
\tag{10.36}\]
Look for solutions \(u (t, x) = u_1 (x) e^{\mathrm{i} \omega t}\) and change variable to \(\tau = (2 x / g)^{1/2}\). Show that Equation 10.36 becomes \[
\frac{1}{\tau} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d} \tau^2} (\tau u_1) + \omega^2 u_1 = 0.
\tag{10.37}\] Find the solution that stays finite at \(x = 0\) and interpret it physically.

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.1 Qualitative Picture
The magnetorotational instability (MRI) was first discovered in the context of plasma fusion reactors by Velikhov (1959) and Chandrasekhar (1961) and then rediscovered in the context of accretion disks by Balbus and Hawley (1991). This is the instability thought to be responsible for the \(\alpha\)-viscosity in many astrophysical systems: from X-ray binaries to AGN disks. It is one of the most important, among the many instabilities operating in plasmas, so we will cover it in detail in these notes.
It was long known that a way to transport angular momentum in the disk is through magnetic stresses, that is the \(B_r B_{\theta} / 4 \pi\) term in the momentum equation. However, to explain the observed luminosities from accretion disks, the magnetic stresses must be similar in magnitude to the pressure in the disk \(p\) (the proportionality constant being the \(\alpha\)-viscosity coefficient). Given a small component of the field in the radial direction, flux freezing can grow \(B_{\theta}\) linearly in time. However, since \(B_r\) is small, this mechanism can transport angular momentum efficiently only if \(B_{\theta}^2 \gg p\). Such a strong toroidal field cannot be contained in the disk. The requirement for the magnetic stresses to do the job of transporting angular momentum is that \(B_r^2 \approx B_{\theta}^2 \approx 4 \pi \rho c_s^2\). Detailed simulations have shown that MRI is a mechanism that naturally produces the required field strengths over a short timescale.
Consider an accretion disk with Keplerian angular velocity profile \[
\Omega (R) = \Omega_0  \left( \frac{R_0}{R} \right)^{3 / 2},
\tag{27.1}\] initially threaded by a vertical magnetic field \(B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be two fluid elements connected by a magnetic field line (initially vertical) and displace their positions according to \(\xi_r = \epsilon \cos k z\), as shown in Figure 27.1. The fluid elements \(A\) and \(B\) immediately accelerate to match the local angular velocity. However, as a result of the change in angular velocity, a toroidal component of the field, \(B_{\theta}\) is generated by the stretching of the original field line.
The magnetic tension then creates an attractive force between \(A\) and \(B\), which has the effect of transporting angular momentum from \(A\) to \(B\). This causes \(A\) to lose angular momentum and sink further inwards, while \(B\) gains angular momentum and starts moving outwards. In turn, because the angular velocity decreases with radius, \(A\) increases its angular velocity, while \(B\) slows down, further separating the two points. This in turn enhances the magnetic tension force. The cycle we have just described is unstable, so the initial perturbation grows exponentially in time, until the system becomes nonlinear.
The mechanism we have just described involves the magnetic tension force, so it is natural to expect a characteristic growth rate of \[
\gamma \approx kv_A, \qquad v_A = \frac{B_z}{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho}} .
\tag{27.2}\] In our derivation, we have assumed the field to be sufficiently weak, so that the displaced fluid elements can acquire the angular velocity of their surroundings. This should be valid as long as \[
\omega_A = kv_A \lesssim \Omega .
\tag{27.3}\] We will find that the exact condition for instability is \(kv_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega\), so the maximum growth rate is achieved by taking \(k\) sufficiently large, so that \(\gamma \approx kv_A \approx \Omega\). This is a very short timescale: the MRI grows over the orbital time scale! Moreover, the growth rate is independent of the field strength, as long as \(v_A\) is not so large that the required \(k\) to satisfy \(kv_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega\) corresponds to perturbation with characteristic size larger than the vertical size of the disk.

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.2 Detailed Calculation
The starting point is the Euler equation, which we write in the usual form in cylindrical coordinates \((R, \theta, z)\): \[
\rho \left[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) \mathbf{v} \right] = - \nabla \left( p + \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} \right) +
\frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{4 \pi} +\mathbf{g} \rho .
\tag{27.4}\] We consider a disk that is Keplerian and threaded by a vertical magnetic field: \[
\mathbf{v}= R \Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} +\mathbf{u}, \qquad \mathbf{B}=
B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} +\mathbf{b}, \qquad p + \frac{B^2}{8 \pi} = P_0 + P.
\tag{27.5}\] We will treat \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) as (small) Eulerian perturbations. We will only consider modes that are axisymmetric (no \(\theta\) dependence) and incompressible \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}= \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial (Ru_r)}{\partial R} +
\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z} = 0.
\tag{27.6}\] To leading order in \(\mathbf{u}\) (using Kepler’s law) \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} &{}\rightarrow{} && (R \Omega)
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla (R
\Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) =  \\
& && - 2 \Omega u_{\theta}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \left( R \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Omega}{\mathrm{d} R} + 2 \Omega \right) u_R \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \\
& && \frac{1}{2} \Omega u_R  \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - 2 \Omega u_{\theta}
\hat{\mathbf{R}} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.7}\] Similarly, \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} &{}\rightarrow{} && B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}}
\cdot \nabla \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b} \cdot \nabla (B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}}) =
\\
& && B_0  \dfrac{\partial b_R}{\partial z}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_0
\frac{\partial b_{\theta}}{\partial z}  \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + B_0
\frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z}  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.8}\] So the linearized momentum equation reads \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2} \Omega u_R
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - 2 \Omega u_{\theta}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} = -
\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla P + B_0  \dfrac{\partial b_R}{\partial z}
\hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_0  \frac{\partial b_{\theta}}{\partial z}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + B_0  \frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z}
\hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{27.9}\] The induction equation can be linearized in a similar way: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \\
& \quad \rightarrow \nabla \times \bigl[(R \Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) \times (b_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + b_{\theta} \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + b_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \\
& \qquad\qquad + (u_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + u_{\theta} \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + u_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \times (B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}})\bigr] \\
& \quad = \nabla \times [- R \Omega b_R \hat{\mathbf{z}} + R \Omega b_z \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - u_R B_0 \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + u_{\theta} B_0 \hat{\mathbf{R}}] \\
& \quad = \nabla \times [ (R \Omega b_z + u_{\theta} B_0) \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - u_R B_0 \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - R \Omega b_R \hat{\mathbf{z}}] \\
& \quad = \left( \frac{\partial u_R}{\partial z} B_0 \right) \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \biggl( R \Omega \frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\theta}}{\partial z} B_0 \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R + \Omega \frac{\partial (Rb_R)}{\partial R} \biggr) \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (Ru_R B_0)}{\partial R} \right] \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\
& \quad = \left( \frac{\partial u_R}{\partial z} B_0 \right) \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \left( \frac{\partial u_{\theta}}{\partial z} B_0 - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R \right) \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (Ru_R B_0)}{\partial R} \right] \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{27.10}\] In the last equation we have also used the condition that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{b}= 0\).
We will consider a small patch of the disk, so that we can use the Fourier (WKB) ansatz: \[
\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}_0 e^{\lambda t + \mathrm{i} (k_R R + k_z z)}, \qquad
\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}_0 e^{\lambda t + \mathrm{i} (k_R R + k_z z)}
\tag{27.11}\] with the additional assumption that \(k_z \gg k_R\). Substituting this into the linearized equations of motions yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda u_r - 2 \Omega u_{\theta} &{}={} && - \mathrm{i} k_R  \frac{P}{\rho} +
\frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 b_r}{4 \pi \rho},  \\
\lambda u_{\theta} + \frac{\Omega}{2} u_r &{}={} && \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0
b_{\theta}}{4 \pi \rho}, \\
\lambda u_z &{}={} && - \mathrm{i} k_z  \frac{P}{\rho} + \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 b_z}{4
\pi \rho} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.12}\] We can eliminate \(P / \rho\) from the last equation and insert it into the first to obtain (in the limit \(k_z \gg k_R\)): \[
\lambda u_r - 2 \Omega u_{\theta} = \mathrm{i} k_z  \frac{B_0 b_r}{4 \pi \rho} .
\tag{27.13}\] The linearized induction equation yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda b_R &{}={} && \mathrm{i} k_z B_0 u_R  \\
\lambda b_{\theta} &{}={} && - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R + \mathrm{i} k_z B_0
u_{\theta} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.14}\] Eliminating \(b_R\) in the second equation yields \[
\lambda b_{\theta} = - \frac{3}{2}  \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 \Omega}{\lambda}
u_R + \mathrm{i} k_z B_0 u_{\theta} .
\tag{27.15}\] Eliminating \(b_{\theta}\) and \(b_R\) in the momentum equations above and introducing \(\omega_A^2 = k_z^2 B_0^2 / 4 \pi \rho\) yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\lambda^2 + \omega_A^2) u_R &{}={} && 2 \lambda \Omega u_{\theta},  \\
(\lambda^2 + \omega_A^2) u_{\theta} &{}={} && \left( - \frac{\lambda}{2} \Omega
+ \frac{3}{2}  \frac{\omega_A^2 \Omega}{\lambda} \right) u_R .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.16}\] Introducing \[
\mu^2 = \lambda^2 + \omega_A^2,
\tag{27.17}\] the dispersion relation becomes \[
f (\mu^2) = \mu^4 + \Omega^2 \mu^2 - 4 \Omega^2 \omega_A^2 = 0.
\tag{27.18}\] The instability is present when the second root of \(f (\mu^2)\) occurs for \(\mu^2 > \omega_A^2\). This occurs if \[
f (\omega_A^2) = \omega_A^4 - 3 \Omega^2 \omega_A^2 < 0 \Longrightarrow
\boxed{\frac{k_z B_0}{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho}} = \omega_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega .}
\tag{27.19}\] We find that if \(k_z\) is sufficiently small (sufficiently large wavelength of the perturbation), then the mode is unstable. However, if the background field is too large, then the condition in Equation 27.19 might only be satisfied for \(k_z\) that corresponds to modes larger than the disk size, so the system is stable.
The growth rate of the instability is found by solving the dispersion relation to find \[
\lambda^2 = \frac{\Omega}{2}  \left( - \Omega + \sqrt{\Omega^2 + 16
\omega_A^2} \right) - \omega_A^2,
\tag{27.20}\] which is maximized when \[
\omega_A = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4} \Omega \approx \Omega,
\tag{27.21}\] which corresponds to \[
k_{\max} \approx \frac{\sqrt{4 \pi \rho}}{B_0} \Omega .
\tag{27.22}\] The growth rate of the most unstable mode is \[
\boxed{\lambda_{\max} = \frac{3}{4} \Omega .}
\tag{27.23}\] It is instructive to check the limit of our analysis when \(B_0 \rightarrow 0\), which corresponds to \(\omega_A \rightarrow 0\). If \(\omega_A \equiv 0\), then Equation 27.16 reduces to \[
\lambda^2 u_R = - \Omega^2 u_R, \qquad \lambda^2 u_{\theta} = - \Omega^2
u_{\theta} .
\tag{27.24}\] That is the perturbations oscillate with the epicyclic frequency \(\Omega\).
In the limit of \(0 < \omega_A \ll \Omega\) (long wavelength perturbations, or weak magnetic field), we can drop all the \(\omega_A\) terms in Equation 27.16, with the exception of the term multiplied by \(\Omega\) to obtain \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda^2 u_R &{}={} && 2 \lambda \Omega u_{\theta},  \\
\lambda^2 u_{\theta} &{}={} && \left( - \frac{\lambda}{2} \Omega + \frac{3}{2}
\frac{\omega_A^2 \Omega}{\lambda} \right) u_R .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.25}\] Eliminating \(u_{\theta}\), we obtain: \[
\lambda^2 u_R = \left( \frac{3 \omega_A^2 \Omega^2}{\lambda^2} - \Omega^2
\right) u_R,
\tag{27.26}\] which has unstable solutions with \(\lambda^2 > 0\) as long as \(\omega_A > 0\).

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.3 In-class worksheet
There is a simple mechanical equivalent of the magnetorotational instability (MRI) in a disk with vertical magnetic field. This model is concerned with two particles of mass \(m\) orbiting a central object with angular velocity \(\Omega = \Omega (R)\) (not necessarily Keplerian). The particles are connected by a spring with spring constant \(mK\), as shown in Figure 27.2.






Figure 27.2: Mechanical analogue of the magnetorotational instability: two masses connected by a spring, orbiting a central object.



The coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) denote the displacement of one of the two masses from the common center of mass.

Assuming \(0 \leq x, y \ll R\), show that the displacement satisfies the differential equations \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\ddot{x} - 2 \Omega \dot{y} &{}={} && - \left( K + \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Omega^2}{\mathrm{d} \log R} \right) x, \\
\ddot{y} + 2 \Omega \dot{x} &{}={} && - Ky.
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.27}\] Note that these are the same equations as those obtained for the MRI in a disk threaded by a vertical magnetic field, \(k_R = 0\), and \(K = (v_A k_z)^2 = \omega_A^2\).
Look for solutions in the form \(x (t) = x_0 e^{\lambda t},\) \(y (t) = y_0 e^{\lambda t}\). Find \(\lambda\).
Under what conditions is the system unstable?
